cards.q: You need to know whether a function throws when its argument is empty. Which kind of document do you want?
cards.a:
Reference, because it describes every case precisely

A tutorial shows one happy path and an explanation discusses ideas. Only the reference page promises to cover every input, edge cases included.

cards.q: You have never used a library and want to get something working. Where do you start?
cards.a:
A tutorial, then the reference for the functions it uses

A tutorial gets you to something working quickly. Then the reference pages tell you exactly what each function you used really does.

cards.q: A forum answer says a function returns -1 on error. How should you treat that?
cards.a:
As a lead to confirm on the reference page

Forum answers can be right, outdated or about a different version. They tell you where to look; the reference page, for the version you are using, decides.

cards.q: Why should a reference page not tell a story?
cards.a:
Its job is to let readers find exact facts quickly, and narrative hides them

Readers arrive with a specific question. A predictable layout of precise facts answers it; a story makes them read everything to find one sentence.

cards.q: You call `trim_left(s, "x")`. Which overload is used?
cards.a:
(1), because a string literal converts to `std::string_view`, not to `char`

`"x"` is an array of two `char`s (with the zero), which converts to `std::string_view`. Only `'x'`, in single quotes, is a `char` and picks (2); a string never converts to a `char`.

cards.q: What does `trim_left("xxx", "x")` return, according to the page?
cards.a:
An empty string, because every character is removed

The function removes every leading character that is in `chars`. When all of them are, nothing is left, and that is a normal result, not an error.

cards.q: What does "may throw `std::bad_alloc`" mean for your code?
cards.a:
It can throw that exception, so code that must not fail has to be ready for it, even if it rarely happens

"May" means it is part of the contract. It will rarely happen, but code that must not fail has to plan for it anyway.

cards.q: Which section should you always skim even when you think you have your answer?
cards.a:
Notes, where the surprises live

Notes (or remarks) are where pages hide "not thread-safe", "not null-terminated", "deprecated" and "behaviour changed in version 3".

cards.q: A parameter is `std::vector<int>& out`. What does that tell you?
cards.a:
The function writes to (or changes) your vector: it is an output or in-out parameter

A non-`const` reference lets the function change your object. Read-only access would be `const std::vector<int>&`; a copy would be `std::vector<int>`.

cards.q: Why does `std::sort` not compile on a `std::list`?
cards.a:
It requires random-access iterators, and a list's iterators are only bidirectional

The template's named requirement, `LegacyRandomAccessIterator`, is part of the signature. A list cannot jump to its middle, so it has its own `list::sort` instead.

cards.q: What does `[[nodiscard]]` on a function tell you?
cards.a:
Ignoring its return value is almost certainly a bug

The compiler warns if you drop the result. Functions like `empty()` and `std::async` are marked this way because ignoring them is a common mistake.

cards.q: `std::map::insert` returns `std::pair<iterator, bool>`. What does the `bool` mean?
cards.a:
Whether the element was actually inserted

If the key already exists, `insert` does not replace the value: the `bool` is false and the iterator points at the existing element.

cards.q: A page says "`n` must be less than `size()`; otherwise the behaviour is undefined". Who is responsible for checking?
cards.a:
You, before calling, because the function does not check

A precondition is your side of the contract. Undefined behaviour means anything can happen, including a crash or silent memory corruption, not just a strange value.

cards.q: A range is `[first, last)` with `first == last`. How many elements does it hold?
cards.a:
None, it is empty

A half-open range includes `first` and excludes `last`, so equal ends mean nothing in between: the standard way to write an empty range.

cards.q: What is the difference between `v[i]` and `v.at(i)` for an index that is too large?
cards.a:
`v[i]` is undefined behaviour; `v.at(i)` throws `std::out_of_range`

`operator[]` has a precondition and no check; `at` checks and reports the error. That difference is written on both reference pages.

cards.q: `push_back` gives the strong guarantee. What does that mean if it throws?
cards.a:
The vector is exactly as it was before the call

The strong guarantee is commit-or-roll-back. "Valid but unspecified" is the weaker basic guarantee.

cards.q: Which is the final word on C++: cppreference or the standard?
cards.a:
The standard; cppreference is a careful community reference that follows it

cppreference is written by volunteers who track the ISO standard closely. When they disagree, the standard decides, and the page usually gets fixed.

cards.q: A member function is marked (C++20). Can you call it when compiling as C++17?
cards.a:
No, it was added in C++20

The marker says when the member appeared in the standard. In C++17 mode it is not declared at all, so the call does not compile.

cards.q: Why not rely on a page's "possible implementation"?
cards.a:
Only the documented behaviour is guaranteed

It is an illustration, not your library's code, and the real library may be implemented differently. Details it happens to show, such as the order of calls, are not promised unless the description says so.

cards.q: What does `std::stoi("  12abc", &used)` set `used` to?
cards.a:
4, because two spaces and two digits were processed

`stoi` skips leading whitespace, reads as many digits as it can and stops at the first character that cannot be part of the number. It throws only when no digits at all could be read.

cards.q: `m.insert({"a", 5})` is called when `m["a"]` is already 1. What is `m["a"]` afterwards?
cards.a:
Still 1, because `insert` does nothing when the key exists

`insert` only inserts a new key; its returned `bool` is false here. To overwrite, use `m["a"] = 5` or `insert_or_assign`. A `std::map` never holds two entries with one key.

cards.q: How do you know `std::from_chars` parsed the whole string?
cards.a:
`ec` is `std::errc{}` and `ptr` equals the end of the input

`from_chars` stops at the first character it cannot use and reports success if it read a number at all. Only `ptr == end` tells you nothing was left over.

cards.q: When would you choose the `std::error_code&` overload of a filesystem function?
cards.a:
When failure is an expected, normal outcome you want to handle without exceptions

A missing file you are about to create, for example, is not exceptional. The `error_code` overload reports it without throwing; the other overload throws `filesystem_error`.

cards.q: What does `std::string::find` return when the text is not found?
cards.a:
`std::string::npos`

`npos` is the largest `size_t` value. Comparing with `-1` happens to work after conversion, but `npos` is what the page documents, and `0` would mean "found at the start".

cards.q: What does "amortised constant" mean for `push_back`?
cards.a:
Constant on average, with an occasional costly reallocation

Most calls just write one element. Every so often the vector reallocates and moves everything, but capacity grows geometrically, so the average cost per call over many calls stays constant.

cards.q: You hold a reference to an element of a `std::map` and insert another element. Is the reference still valid?
cards.a:
Yes, because inserting into a map invalidates nothing

Map nodes never move: rebalancing changes links, not where elements live. The map's page says insert invalidates no iterators or references.

cards.q: What is wrong with `v.erase(it); ++it;`?
cards.a:
`it` is invalid after `erase`, so use the iterator `erase` returns

After erasing, `it` must not be used at all, not even incremented. `it = v.erase(it);` gives a valid iterator to the element after the erased one.

cards.q: Does `push_back` always invalidate every iterator of a vector?
cards.a:
Only when it reallocates; otherwise only `end()` changes

A reallocation happens when the size would exceed the capacity. Without one the elements stay put, so existing iterators remain valid and only the past-the-end iterator changes.

cards.q: A member is marked (since C++20) and your project uses `/std:c++17`. What happens if you call it?
cards.a:
It does not compile, because it is not declared in C++17 mode

The standard library hides declarations that belong to later standards when you compile for an earlier one, so the name simply is not there.

cards.q: Why might `__cplusplus` say `199711L` on MSVC even in C++20 mode?
cards.a:
MSVC keeps the old value unless `/Zc:__cplusplus` is given

For compatibility, MSVC reports the 1997 value by default. `_MSVC_LANG` has the real one, or pass `/Zc:__cplusplus` to get the correct value.

cards.q: Where do you find a feature-test macro's name?
cards.a:
In the Notes section of the feature's reference page

Each page names the macro, such as `__cpp_lib_format`, and the value that marks support. cppreference also has a full table of library feature-test macros.

cards.q: What does `std::format("[{:6}]", "ab")` produce?
cards.a:
`[ab    ]`, because strings align left by default

The format specification on the page says strings are left-aligned and numbers right-aligned unless you give `<`, `>` or `^`.

cards.q: `nSize` is described as a size in characters. You have `wchar_t buffer[260]`. What do you pass?
cards.a:
260, `std::size(buffer)`, not `sizeof(buffer)`, which is 520

Characters are not bytes: each `wchar_t` is 2 bytes. The page asks for characters and its remarks say the function itself handles the null within that count.

cards.q: `GetModuleFileNameW` returns exactly `nSize`. What happened?
cards.a:
The buffer was too small and the path was truncated

On success the return value is the length without the null, which is always less than `nSize`. Returning `nSize` is the page's signal for truncation.

cards.q: What does a null `hModule` mean for this function?
cards.a:
The executable file of the current process

The Parameters section says that if `hModule` is `NULL`, the function retrieves the path of the current process's executable file.

cards.q: What is the difference between the Library and DLL lines in the requirements?
cards.a:
You link against the library; the DLL is loaded at run time

`Kernel32.lib` tells the linker how to import the function; `Kernel32.dll` holds the code the loader maps into your process.

cards.q: What does `_In_opt_` on a parameter tell you?
cards.a:
The function only reads it, and null is allowed

`_In_` means read-only input and `_opt_` means `NULL` is accepted. You still have to pass something, as C has no way to leave an argument out.

cards.q: A function takes `_Out_writes_bytes_(cb)`. You have a buffer of 50 `wchar_t`s. What do you pass as `cb`?
cards.a:
100 (50 × `sizeof(wchar_t)`), the size in bytes

The `_bytes_` form counts bytes; plain `_Out_writes_` counts elements. Passing 50 here would tell the function the buffer is half its real size.

cards.q: `GetEnvironmentVariableW` returns 12 for a buffer of 10 characters. What does 12 mean?
cards.a:
The buffer is too small: 12 characters, including the null, are needed

This is the size-query pattern: a return value bigger than the buffer means "too small, here is what you need". Allocate 12 and call again.

cards.q: Why should a size-query-then-fetch sequence be a loop?
cards.a:
The value may change between the calls and need a bigger buffer the second time

Another thread or process can change the value between your two calls. Loop until the fetch fits.

cards.q: A function returns `S_FALSE`. Did it fail?
cards.a:
No, `S_FALSE` is a success code meaning "no"

`S_FALSE` is 1, with the severity bit clear, so `SUCCEEDED` is true; it means "no" or "nothing to do". That is why you test with `SUCCEEDED`/`FAILED`, not by comparing with `S_OK`.

cards.q: What Win32 error is inside the HRESULT `0x80070002`?
cards.a:
2, `ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND` (facility 7 means Win32)

`0x8007xxxx` is `HRESULT_FROM_WIN32`: severity bit set, facility 7 (Win32), and the low 16 bits are the Win32 code, here 2.

cards.q: A registry function returns 5. Should you call `GetLastError`?
cards.a:
No: registry functions return the error code directly, and 5 is `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`

The page's Return value section says which system a function uses. Registry functions return a `LSTATUS` code and do not set the last error.

cards.q: What severity does the NTSTATUS `0xC0000005` have?
cards.a:
Error, because its top two bits are `11`

`0xC` is `1100` in binary, so the top two bits are 3: error. `0xC0000005` is `STATUS_ACCESS_VIOLATION`.

cards.q: Why must you set `cbSize` before calling a function that takes the structure?
cards.a:
It tells the function which version of the structure you have

Newer Windows versions add members to the end. `cbSize` tells the function how many of them your program knows about, so it reads and writes only those and never touches memory past your structure.

cards.q: A page says "can be one of the following values". May you combine two with `|`?
cards.a:
No, it takes a single value

"One of" means an enumerated value, not a set of bit flags. OR-ing two such values produces some other number, which may be a third value or invalid.

cards.q: What should you put in a member documented as "reserved; must be zero"?
cards.a:
Zero, for example by initialising with `{}`

Reserved members may get a meaning in a later Windows version. Leaving garbage there could ask for behaviour you never intended; zero-initialising the whole structure with `{}` takes care of it.

cards.q: What does `#define _WIN32_WINNT 0x0A00` do?
cards.a:
Tells the Windows headers you target Windows 10, making declarations up to that version available

It is a compile-time switch for the headers. It does not check the version at run time; your program can still be started on older Windows and fail there.

cards.q: Can you call `sorted([3, 1], None, True)`?
cards.a:
No, `key` and `reverse` are keyword-only

In the signature `sorted(iterable, /, *, key=None, reverse=False)`, everything after `*` must be passed by name: `sorted([3, 1], reverse=True)`.

cards.q: What does `"a,,b".split(",")` return, and how is that different from `"a  b".split()`?
cards.a:
`['a', '', 'b']`; with no separator you get `['a', 'b']`

With an explicit separator, every occurrence splits, so two commas give an empty string between them. With no separator, runs of whitespace count as one and empty strings are dropped.

cards.q: What does a "CPython implementation detail" note mean for your code?
cards.a:
It holds for the reference interpreter only

Other implementations, such as PyPy, may behave differently, and CPython itself may change it. Do not rely on it.

cards.q: Why is `x = x.sort()` a bug?
cards.a:
`sort()` sorts in place and returns `None`

The list is sorted, but then `x` is set to the `None` that `sort()` returns. Use `x.sort()` alone, or `x = sorted(x)` for a new list.

cards.q: What does `parseInt("12.5kg")` return?
cards.a:
`12`, stopping at the first non-digit

`parseInt` reads digits until the first character that cannot be part of an integer, here the `.`, and ignores the rest. `parseFloat` would give 12.5.

Without a compare function, elements are compared as strings

As strings, `"1" < "10" < "9"`. Pass a compare function, `sort((a, b) => a - b)`, to sort numbers by value.

cards.q: Should production code use an API marked Stability: 1?
cards.a:
Better not: experimental APIs may change or vanish

Node's stability index runs 0 (deprecated), 1 (experimental), 2 (stable) and 3 (legacy). Experimental APIs can change or be removed in any release.

cards.q: Why compare `err.code` instead of `err.message` in Node?
cards.a:
Codes are documented and stable; messages can change

Error codes such as `ENOENT` or `ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE` are a documented interface. Message texts are for people and may be reworded in any version.

cards.q: A function returns `const T*` and has no documentation. What can you assume about ownership?
cards.a:
Probably that you do not own it, but check

Nothing is certain without documentation, but a `const T*` usually means borrowed: do not delete it. Look for a comment, tests or the implementation to confirm how long it lives.

cards.q: `findInt` returns an empty optional. What two situations could that mean?
cards.a:
The key is missing, or its value is not a complete integer

An empty optional only says "no result". Its doc comment says both reasons give the same result; use `find` first if you must tell them apart.

cards.q: Why look at a project's tests when its docs are thin?
cards.a:
They show intended use and edge cases, and they really run

Tests are examples that the build checks, so they match the code's real behaviour, edge cases included.

cards.q: You find in the source that a function happens to sort its output. May you rely on that?
cards.a:
Not safely, because it is not documented

Undocumented behaviour may change in the next version. If you must rely on it, pin it with a test of your own so you notice when it changes.

cards.q: `man open` shows a shell command page. How do you get the system call?
cards.a:
`man 2 open`

System calls are in section 2 of the manual. Asking for the section number first picks that page instead of the command in section 1.

cards.q: A spec says senders SHOULD NOT send trailing whitespace. Must a receiver handle it?
cards.a:
Yes, senders may still do it with good reason

RFC 2119's SHOULD NOT is a strong recommendation, not a ban: a sender may have a valid reason to do it. A robust receiver therefore copes.

cards.q: What does `1*DIGIT` mean in ABNF?
cards.a:
One or more digits

In ABNF, `n*m` means between n and m repetitions; `1*` with no upper bound is one or more. `*DIGIT` alone would be zero or more.

cards.q: How do you find corrections to a published RFC?
cards.a:
In its errata, and in newer RFCs that update it

RFCs are never changed once published. Corrections are listed as errata, and later RFCs that update or obsolete it are noted in its header.

cards.q: Why run an example unchanged before adapting it?
cards.a:
So later problems are known to come from your changes

Running it first confirms it works in your environment. If it then breaks after your edits, you know where to look.
cards.lessonTitle: Turning an Example into Your Code

cards.q: An example calls `read` once. When is that not enough?
cards.a:
When a read can return fewer bytes than requested

Many read functions may return less than you asked for, for example from a pipe or a socket, or near the end. Real code loops until it has everything or reaches the end.
cards.lessonTitle: Turning an Example into Your Code

cards.q: How do you make sure a handle is closed on every error path?
cards.a:
Wrap it in an RAII object whose destructor closes it

A destructor runs on every way out of the scope, early returns and exceptions included, so no path can forget the close.
cards.lessonTitle: Turning an Example into Your Code

cards.q: What is wrong with `std::string(buffer, n)` when `n` can be -1?
cards.a:
-1 becomes a huge `size_t`, so it reads far past the buffer

The length parameter is unsigned, so -1 converts to the largest `size_t`. Check the error value before using it as a length.
cards.lessonTitle: Turning an Example into Your Code

cards.q: Why write down a prediction before running an experiment?
cards.a:
So you notice when the result surprises you

A surprise is when you learn something. Without a prediction written first, it is easy to tell yourself afterwards that you expected whatever happened.

cards.q: What does `std::nearbyint(2.5)` return by default, and why?
cards.a:
2.0, because halves round to the even neighbour

`nearbyint` uses the current rounding mode, which by default is round-to-nearest-even. `std::round` is the one that rounds halves away from zero.

cards.q: What is a learning test?
cards.a:
A test that pins down library behaviour you rely on

It turns an experiment into a check that keeps running, so when the library is upgraded and that behaviour changes, a test fails instead of your program.

cards.q: An experiment reading one element past the end of a vector prints 0. What have you learned?
cards.a:
Nothing you can rely on: it is undefined behaviour

Undefined behaviour can print 0 today and crash elsewhere or tomorrow. Experiments only tell you about behaviour the documentation defines.

cards.q: An example from the docs does not compile. What do you check first?
cards.a:
Whether the docs match your installed version

Most mismatches between docs and behaviour come from reading the documentation for a different version than the one you have.
cards.lessonTitle: When the Docs Are Wrong or Missing

cards.q: You upgrade a library from 1.4 to 3.1. Which changelog entries should you read?
cards.a:
Every release from 1.4 to 3.1, major ones above all

Changes accumulate across every release in between. The major versions 2.0 and 3.0 are where breaking changes are most likely, but smaller releases can deprecate things too.
cards.lessonTitle: When the Docs Are Wrong or Missing

cards.q: What makes a good documentation bug report?
cards.a:
The page, what it says, a minimal program and the version

Maintainers need to see the exact section, what it claims, what really happens with a minimal program they can run, and which version you used.
cards.lessonTitle: When the Docs Are Wrong or Missing

cards.q: How should you treat a function an AI assistant suggests?
cards.a:
As a lead to check on its reference page, then test

Suggestions can name functions that do not exist or behave differently. Confirm it on its reference page and test it, as you would a forum answer.
cards.lessonTitle: When the Docs Are Wrong or Missing

cards.q: Why should a doc comment say what a function does rather than how?
cards.a:
So the implementation can change without the docs going wrong

The contract is what readers can rely on. Describing the implementation ties the documentation to details that will change.

cards.q: A parameter is a timeout. What must its documentation include?
cards.a:
Its unit and allowed values, including 0 and negatives

Without a unit, 1000 could be milliseconds or seconds. Readers also need to know what 0 or a negative value means: wait forever, fail at once, or an error.

cards.q: What belongs in a changelog entry for a breaking change?
cards.a:
What changed and what users must do, marked as breaking

Users need to know what broke and how to adapt their code. Breaking changes belong in a new major version and should be clearly marked.

cards.q: How can tests help keep documentation true?
cards.a:
Each documented behaviour becomes a test that fails if it changes

Turn each documented behaviour, especially each error case, into a test. A change that makes the documentation wrong then fails the build.
